Quick Read

A trader used AI and Python to test more than 100 trading strategies and 700 variations. Most failed once trading costs and real-world conditions were factored in.

One strategy won 69% of its trades but returned just 16.9% over 10 years, compared with 214.9% for simply holding the S&P 500. Even the few promising strategies offered no guaranteed edge.

Sponsored: AI Can Give You a Trading Answer. But Can You See the Data Behind It? Explore Visual Sectors' Options Intel, which brings together 25 market indicators and historical stock analysis to help traders evaluate potential moves.

A trader spent weeks testing more than 100 trading strategies and roughly 700 variations, hoping to find approaches that could consistently beat the stock market. With the help of AI, they built a Python program to test everything from chart patterns and insider buying to machine learning models and AI-powered stock predictions.

The results weren't encouraging. Most strategies failed once real trading costs and other factors were included. And the trader found the reasons behind those failures more useful than the handful of strategies that appeared to work.

Don't Miss:

AI Can Write The Code. But Can It Understand The Code? This Startup Is Building The Missing Layer.

Teachers, Nurses And First Responders Are Being Priced Out Of The Communities They Serve. That's putting a different part of the housing market in the spotlight.

"Most of it didn't survive," the trader wrote on Reddit's r/algotrading forum recently. "Writing this up because the reasons they died were more useful to me than the few that worked."

Why So Many Strategies Failed

One of the biggest surprises was how little a high win rate actually meant. A strategy that bought the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY), an exchange-traded fund tracking the S&P 500, won 69% of its trades but returned just 16.9% over 10 years. Simply holding SPY during that period would have returned 214.9%.

Trading costs were another problem. One machine learning model appeared to beat its group of stocks by 13.2% annually before costs. But when trading costs increased, that advantage dropped to just 2.4%.

Even popular chart patterns struggled. Several setups performed no better than buying stocks at random, despite producing what looked like promising results.

QQQ has dropped about 8% in November and SPY about 5%, leaving the Nasdaq on pace for its worst November since 2008.

The Nasdaq needs a roughly 5% two-day gain to beat 2011's record loss, a move that has happened 36 times since 2008.

QQQ carries more risk than SPY because its top holdings, NVIDIA, Apple and Micron, are most exposed to AI and interest-rate pressures.

The Nasdaq Composite closed on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, at 23,585.80. It is now down 7.28% from its October 30 close of 25,437.00. Markets were closed for Thanksgiving, so two sessions remain: a half day on Friday that ends at 1 p.m. ET, and Monday, November 30, when the month's result is set.

Mario Tama / Getty Images News via Getty Images

At that pace, the index is on track for its worst November since 2008. That year it fell 10.77%, from 1,720.95 to 1,535.57. From 2009 through 2025, no November was worse than the 2.39% loss in 2011.

If you own the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ), which tracks the Nasdaq-100, your losses are larger. Through Wednesday, QQQ fell from $690.49 to $633.93, down 8.19%. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) fell 5.16%, to $716.70.

Futures rose late Thursday, so the Composite can still avoid a record, although the forces behind the selloff remain in place.

What Two Sessions Would Have to Deliver

To finish ahead of 2011, the Composite needs to close Monday above about 24,830. That would take a 5.27% gain over the two sessions combined. Finishing the month flat would take 7.85%, while another 3.77% drop, to about 22,697, would make it worse than 2008.

title: Goldman Sachs Drops Stark Take on Year-End Stock Rally
detail:
Goldman Sachs Drops Stark Take on Year-End Stock Rally
Moz Farooque ACCA
Fri, November 27, 2026 at 6:36 AM PST 2 min read
GS
^GSPC
QQQ
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Goldman Sachs (NYSE:GS) says hedge funds are increasingly focused on protecting their capital rather than chasing stock market gains, casting doubt on the prospects of a year-end rally for the S&P 500 (SPY) and Nasdaq-100 (NASDAQ:QQQ).

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 6 Warning Signs with GS.

Is GS fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

GS GF Value chart

Following October's market rout and November's heightened volatility, professional money managers are scaling back their exposure to stocks and adding bearish positions to their portfolios.Vincent Lin, Goldman Sachs' co-head of prime broking insights and analytics, believes hedge funds are becoming increasingly defensive as 2026 draws to a close.

The shift comes after a strong first half of the year for many hedge funds, with subsequent market turbulence making it increasingly difficult to protect those gains.

Interestingly, hedge fund equity exposure has fallen to multiyear lows, while mutual funds continue attracting fresh capital, according to Goldman Sachs.

That divergence suggests institutional investors and other market participants are approaching the recent selloff differently. One particularly striking development was last week's 19-percentage-point increase in short positioning through exchange-traded funds, the third-largest weekly increase recorded by Goldman Sachs over the past decade.

Hedge funds are also targeting homebuilders while increasing exposure to defensive areas, including consumer staples (XLP) and utilities (XLU).

Meanwhile, ETFs and mutual funds collectively attracted $150 billion in fresh investments over the past month despite falling stock prices.

Lin also noted a shift in technology investing away from infrastructure providers toward companies capable of monetizing artificial intelligence, including Amazon (AMZN), Microsoft (MSFT), Alphabet (GOOGL) and Meta Platforms (META).

Investors Takeaway

For Americans investing through their 401(k)s and retirement accounts, the divergence between household investment flows and hedge fund positioning is particularly noteworthy.

However, defensive positioning does not necessarily signal another imminent market selloff. Stabilizing stock prices could encourage professional investors to rebuild their exposure, supporting a recovery.

December's inflation and employment reports, alongside the Federal Reserve's next interest rate decision, could prove decisive in determining whether stocks recover before year-end.

Technology investors should also monitor spending commitments and earnings expectations as Wall Street increasingly prioritizes profitability over ambitious growth projections.

Friday, November 27th, 2026

Major big-box retailers are offering sales of up to -70% on merchandise today, as "Black Friday" kicks off shopping season for the 2026 holidays. Of course, unless you've been living under a rock, you already know advertisements for the Christmas holiday have been going full-bore since the day after Halloween, but today marks the traditional day on the calendars when retail shops are finally able to reach profitability for the year, thereby switching from red ink in their ledgers to black.

According to a report from the ICSC this morning, in-store shopping — as opposed to simply buying on-line — is expected to reach its highest level since 2019, with +84% of American shoppers visiting stores in person this holiday season. Adobe forecasts $12.9 billion will be spent today, up +9.2% year over year. Despite inflation crimping household economies across the nation, holiday shopping looks to be non-negotiable.

Pre-market futures are in the positive at this hour — +124 points in the S&P 500, +679 on the Dow and +639 on the tech-heavy Nasdaq — following a mixed session on Wednesday. These numbers came up off the mat mid-day Wednesday, when notoriously bearish hedge fund manager Michael Burry declared himself "long" on the market from here. In honor of the long Thanksgiving weekend today, Wall Street's stock market closes at 1 pm ET today.

Goods Deficit, Inventories Both Escalate in October

Advanced U.S. Trade in Goods for October is out this morning, sinking by a $14 billion wider margin between imports and exports to a deficit of -$149.5 billion. This follows the downwardly revised -$135.1 billion from the prior month, and is the second-lowest print since the all-time low -$159 billion in March of 2025 (directly ahead of President Trump's heavy tariff "Liberation Day" on April 2nd of last year).

Imports in the month reached an all-time high $365.3 billion, up +6.1% month over month, while Exports also grew, albeit by a lesser margin: +3.2% to $215.8 billion. Of course, much of this is seasonal as companies prepared for holiday shopping season last month, fighting through ever-moving tariff policy and keeping imports at higher prices. The cumulative goods trade deficit added $100 billion to $1.1 trillion from a year ago.

Meanwhile, Retail Inventories for October climbed +0.8% to $893.2 billion in this morning's report. This follows an upwardly revised +0.7% from September, and up +5.1% year over year. For Wholesale Inventories, these have ratcheted up +0.9% from a +0.5% estimate for its ninth-straight monthly increase to $943.4 billion, +8.5% year over year.
